title: Digital ethics: Existing duties extend to new media
desc: Applies competence, confidentiality and notification duties contextually while separating metadata inspection, privilege and remedial obligations.

kps.k: Digital practice extends existing competence and confidentiality duties rather than creating a guarantee of technological safety.
kps.d: The ABA Commission frames technological awareness as part of existing competence and proposes making reasonable protection against inadvertent disclosure, unauthorized disclosure and unauthorized access explicit in Model Rule 1.6(c). It argues that technology can improve service quality, affordability and access, but supplies normative guidance rather than empirical evidence of those benefits. A breach alone would not establish a rule violation. The Florida packet similarly connects electronic-document safeguards to existing state confidentiality and competence duties.

qs.q: Comment [6] already encompasses an obligation to remain aware of changes in technology that affect law practice, but the Commission concluded that making this explicit, by addition of the phrase “including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology,” would offer greater clarity in this area and emphasize the importance of technology to modern law practice.
qs.a: ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20, Resolution 105A and Report: Technology and Confidentiality · Regulators & courts · 2012

qs.q: In order to maintain confidentiality under Rule 4-1.6(a), Florida lawyers must take reasonable steps to protect confidential information in all types of documents and information that leave the lawyers’ offices, including electronic documents and electronic communications with other lawyers and third parties.

kps.k: Reasonable security depends on information sensitivity, practical constraints, client choices and independent legal obligations.
kps.d: The revised ABA resolution does not invariably require special transmission security when a communication method affords a reasonable expectation of privacy, but special circumstances can justify stronger measures. Relevant considerations include sensitivity, legal or contractual privacy protections, implementation difficulty and effects on representation. Clients may demand additional safeguards or give informed consent to specified departures from the Model Rules’ baseline; separate privacy and breach-notification law can impose additional duties. Sharing information with outside nonlawyers also requires attention to Rule 5.3 guidance.

kps.k: Prompt notification of inadvertent receipt is distinct from permission to inspect metadata, where ethics authorities disagree.
kps.d: The ABA materials require sender notification when a receiving lawyer knows or reasonably should know that representation-related information was inadvertently sent, including unintended attachments and metadata. The Commission reports that ABA Formal Opinion 06-442 permits metadata review under Rule 4.4 without consent or court authority, while other opinions take the opposite position; its proposal leaves that disagreement unresolved. Florida Opinion 06-2 directs recipients not to seek client information in metadata they know or should know was unintended and to notify the sender if they inadvertently obtain it. That advisory opinion is nonbinding and excludes discovery metadata.

kps.k: Notification does not resolve privilege, return or deletion duties, and deliberate acquisition requires separate analysis.
kps.d: The ABA commentary and Florida packet leave mandatory return and privilege waiver to applicable law; absent a legal requirement, voluntary return or deletion ordinarily rests with professional judgment. Neither treats the inadvertent-disclosure rule as resolving duties concerning material improperly obtained by its sender. In a separate scenario involving documents deliberately obtained by a client without permission, the Florida packet requires disclosure to the opposing party before retention, review or use, directs withdrawal if the client refuses disclosure, and warns of possible disqualification and client sanctions. These scenario-specific directions should not become a general rule for accidental receipt.

kps.k: The practical response centers on continuing education and information-handling controls across electronic practice.
kps.d: The Florida packet identifies hidden authorship data, revisions and prior versions as concrete confidentiality risks and points lawyers to metadata-removal resources. It says safe transmission and receipt may require continuing technology education. The ABA Commission recommends continuously updated security guidance, screens covering electronic as well as tangible information, and communication duties that apply across media. These materials establish a general digital-practice framework; the supplied excerpts do not provide AI-specific performance findings or safeguards merely because the Florida packet also includes generative-AI opinions.

qs.q: Examples of metadata that may be hidden in Microsoft documents include the name of the author, the identification of the computer on which the document was typed, the names of previous document authors and revisions to the document, including prior versions of a final document.

vlens.an: The selected regulators and professional bodies support the proposition that established competence, confidentiality and notification duties extend contextually to digital media rather than creating a guarantee of technological safety. Across the ABA materials and Florida guidance, the common rationale is that lawyers must take reasonable, risk-sensitive precautions, maintain sufficient technological competence and promptly notify senders of known inadvertent disclosures. They also preserve boundaries between distinct legal questions: notification does not itself determine privilege waiver, return or deletion obligations, and wrongfully obtained material requires separate analysis. Material internal variation concerns metadata inspection: the ABA Commission records conflicting ethics opinions and leaves the issue unresolved, whereas Florida Opinion 06-2 directs recipients not to seek unintended client information in metadata. The Florida position is also expressly advisory and excludes discovery metadata. These differences qualify scope and implementation but do not undermine the shared proposition. Because the corpus is curated, this finding characterises only the supplied institutional sources and should not be read as representing all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources directly support the proposition that established professional duties extend contextually to digital media rather than being replaced by technology-specific guarantees. Both ABA Commission materials treat technological awareness as part of competence, require reasonable precautions for client information, and extend inadvertent-disclosure notification to electronically stored information. They also preserve important boundaries: security obligations depend on circumstances and client choices; a breach alone does not prove misconduct; and notification does not determine privilege, return, deletion, wrongful acquisition, or whether metadata may be inspected. The principal internal variation is functional rather than oppositional: the Resolution and Report explains and proposes the doctrinal updates, while the Revised Resolution states the resulting rule language and commentary more directly. The Report additionally foregrounds potential quality, cost, and access benefits and the need for continuing guidance, but these are normative claims rather than empirical findings. It also expressly leaves disagreement over metadata inspection unresolved.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that established professional duties extend contextually to digital media. It applies Florida confidentiality and competence rules to electronic documents, requiring reasonable safeguards rather than technological perfection. It also reinforces the synthesis’s separation of distinct issues: inadvertent metadata exposure triggers notification duties, while return and privilege questions remain matters of applicable law, and deliberately or wrongfully obtained documents require separate analysis. Material qualifications concern scope rather than direction: Opinion 06-2 is advisory and nonbinding, excludes discovery metadata, and does not itself determine waiver or mandatory return. Because the curated evidence for this period contains one source packet, this assessment describes that source alone and does not indicate prevalence among 2025 authorities.
